context: It suffices to consider factors of 1, 2, and 3 when looking for an optimal split. This figure examines a split that already contains three twos, leaving all other factors unchanged.
description: At the top, a gray bar represents the full length n. In the middle row, three adjacent blue pieces labeled “2” have total length 6 and sit to the left of a gray remainder. The bottom row shows just the same left interval of length 6, now filled by two purple pieces labeled “3.” The gray remainder appears only in the middle row and plays no part in the change. A solid gray arrow points down from the three twos to the two threes. The caption reads “Whenever there are three twos, greedily replace them with two threes.”

frames.explanation: Three twos have product 8, and two threes have product 9, while both sums equal 6. Let P be the product of all other positive integer factors, taking P = 1 if there are none. The substitution shown raises the whole product from 8P to 9P, so an optimal split contains at most two twos.
frames.title: Replacing three twos with two threes

summary: Compare two ways to split a length of 6: three twos or two threes.
title: Replacing three twos with two threes
